utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances? MR.. NIEMANN: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Turone, Ms. McHenry and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the Defence appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you. MR.. OLUJIC: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Michael Greaves. MR.. KARABDIC: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman. Cynthia McMurrey and I appear here today on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am very sad to announce this morning on behalf of the Tribunal as a whole and members of the Trial Chamber the passing away yesterday night of Judge Li, one of the judges of this Tribunal, at the age of 91. His age has not been of any effect to his excellent performance. At 91, his thinking is as clear as when he first did his degree in 1922. He is one of the most energetic human beings I have come across. He has been with us all along, he is a foundation member of the Tribunal, and was all through the formulation of the Rules and in every aspect of the regulations, a participant in almost all the committees set up for considering all of the regulations we are using in this Tribunal. Incidentally, he is not -- he did not seek re-election, he had decided not to continue, but suddenly he got ill and was in a local hospital here. The last information we heard was that he was recovering and things were going fine, but all of a sudden, this morning when I came to work, I got information that he had died. In certain respects, for people of that age, it is not too surprising, but in contrast, a person of his energy and willingness to work and assist, it is a little surprising. We will hear a few things: he used to exercise every morning, take a cold bath, so in every respect he was much fitter than his age, but unfortunately this is what has happened to us. We miss him very, very dearly, even if he has to leave us in this way. We knew he would, but at least while he was with us, he was a very close friend, very good companion and helpful in every way in which a colleague can be helpful. I should inform the Trial Chamber and the participants here of our sorrow this morning. He has his family here, and we hope every arrangement might be made to enable them to get back to China. The Trial Chamber would wish us to have at least a minute's silence in his honour before we continue the deliberations of this morning. May this gentleman so rest in perfect peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecution, we would also wish to express our condolences in the very sad departure of Judge Li. We knew of him fondly as a great jurist, a man of great skill and dedication to the rule of law, and to ensure that all parties accused would receive a fair and just trial. His untimely departure is indeed sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I never had Judge Li, I did see him around and I read his opinions, which I think are -- they are such well written opinions, well thought out opinions and to see him in the condition -- physical condition at age 91, it is amazing. He was an amazing person and a great jurist and I think on behalf of all of the Defence we wish his family well and give them our personal condolences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to say that your announcement this morning reminds us all once again, I think, of the transitory nature of this life and how at any moment it is unpredictable. Our life will be judged. Without further ado, I know that those who knew Judge Li well will miss him a great deal. I think all of us as we sit here this morning would wish that we could have the long life that he had and maintain the pure brilliance that he maintained through all of his 91 years. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Your Honours, my submission will be complete, I hope, in about 30 minutes. I have not much more to say in relation to these matters. We have considered the remarks of your Honours in relation to the question of the miscounting of the videotapes. I have certain parts of the transcript that I can take your Honours to, which I wish to take your Honours to, in relation to this question, where it was raised and what was said about it. I think that helps in some clarification of the issue. We have an additional basis upon which we would argue renders these documents admissible, apart from the fact that they are found on the premises. They were shown to certain people who we would say would be in a position to authenticate them and they then could be tendered on that basis, having regard to the fact that one of the exhibits, already an exhibit of General Pasalic, has already been admitted on that basis. It would be on the two bases I think -- when I take your Honours to the transcript, which I will do now, I think any need to call any further evidence would be obviated by that. I do not think we can actually take it any further. I think we have reached the point where not much more can be said about it than what was done. If I may, firstly in relation to the evidence of the witness Moerbauer, in his evidence-in-chief, he was asked by my learned colleague Mr. Turone about this on page 3558, line 16 of the transcript, on the first occasion. My colleague asked the question: "Were there any videotapes among the INDA-BAU material? Answer: Yes, a large number of videotapes were seized. Question: As far as you can remember, how many videotapes were seized in the INDA-BAU premises? Answer: About 50 videotapes. There were a few problems and apparently there was a miscount, but roughly 50, 51. It said 51 and then it turned out to be 54." Mr. Turone then went on on page 3559 to ask the question: "So you have been saying about some mistakes in the counting of the videotapes. What kind of a mistake in the counting of the videotapes took place? When was it corrected, if at any time? Can you explain this point? Answer: Well, on the basis of the file Taubergasse 15, Door 10, I think in that instance, it was corrected right away. That was noted into the record, by the way." Your Honours will know that we are not tendering any videotapes or material from that address. He then goes on: "With regard to the INDA-BAU, that was corrected subsequently." Then later on in the transcript, in the cross-examination of the witness Moerbauer by Madam Residovic, she said to him: "Mr. Moerbauer, is it correct that in some reports, the Bericht or information of seized documents you noted contained errors recording the number of seized videotapes?" The witness then answered in very similar terms: "Concerning the number of seized videotapes, the first note of items seized from Taubergasse 15, Door 14, the first error was discovered by a colleague and was corrected, and the seized videotapes from Koppstrasse 14 [the INDA-BAU premises] were discovered and marked. The error was realised at a later stage and was noted by me in a report." Again in cross-examination of the witness, the witness says at page 3724, line 6: "The videotapes from the INDA-BAU company, there were always 54 of them. There were apparently 54 of them. They were only counted later and they were marked. With regard to a reference to them and giving them a name, that only happened later in the course of processing." Then Moerbauer was asked: "Mr. Moerbauer, I am looking at the second page of the Niederschrift from INDA-BAU and to me it is obvious that it states 51 cassettes. What I am interested in is: which three cassettes did you find later and what are the names of these cassettes, can you tell me that? Answer: In the box, there was apparently always those 54 videotapes, but after hand-over, they were not counted. It was when we had labelled them consecutively that we realised that there were 54 and not 51. Now they were not given a name at once, it was only in the coarse of one and a half to two weeks of analysis that the contents of the videotapes was indicated in a report, along with the contents, along with the reference." Again in cross-examination of the witness Moerbauer, he is asked again about this question, and he says at page 3740 at line 11: "At INDA-BAU, 51, according to the record, were found there, and in fact we found that there were really 54 videotapes there. Now it is the original record we did not refer to the individual tapes by name." So, your Honours, that is the evidence of the witness Moerbauer in relation to that question. In relation to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How did you understand all this you have read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did I understand it? The state of the evidence, your Honour, from that witness at least, is this: that he admits there was a mistake, it was one of the questions that Judge Jan asked me yesterday, why was it not put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was put to one of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is Navrat who made the recoveries, who counted them. I was just referring to the evidence of Navrat, not to Moerbauer. He saw these tapes much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the witness Navrat, he says, at page 5705 of the transcript, in cross-examination: "We have gone from 51 to 54 videos, correct? Answer: That is right. Question: That is a discrepancy of three, correct? Answer: That is right. Question: One possibility is that three videos were added to the original 51; you would accept that possibility, would you not? Answer: Everything is possible, but I have a tough time imagining that. Question: Another possibility is that we were dealing with 54 different videos from the ones that came from INDA-BAU? Answer: That is not right. Question: They were not marked, the containers were not marked, it was not sealed; you accept the possibility, do you not? Answer: I can rule out the possibility." I think that is a misprint, it should be cannot rule out the possibility: "In fact, the cardboard box which left INDA-BAU may not be the same one that arrived at police headquarters because it was not marked either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He did say it was in his custody until he brought it into police headquarters." Next question: "We know for sure that the number of the videos inside the box changed, do we not, between the time -- ? Answer: That is right. Question: Maybe your colleagues were looking through a different cardboard box? Answer: I have a tough time imagining that. Question: If the videotapes changed, perhaps the documents changed too, between the time you brought it and the time your colleagues examined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you not leave that for argument stage, instead of putting it to the witness?" So, your Honours, in terms of what the witnesses can tell us about the matter, I would not think that there is much more that can be said. I think they have said all that there is and I think the position clearly is that they are saying, they are asserting that the original number was 54, it was always 54 that was seized by Navrat, that there was a miscounting at the time of the search, instead of counting 54 there was 51, and that that was subsequently discovered some days later and corrected. I think that emerges clearly from the transcript as to what their position is, so I do not think we would be much assisted from hearing further from them on the point. I think that is as much as they can tell us. There was, however, in our submission, a further basis on which these videos can be tendered. In our submission, the evidence is the evidence and we cannot take it any further than to say to you that the state of the evidence in relation to the confusion on numbers is as clear as it can be, and that there is a discrepancy and any other explanation given will not advance the matter any further. If that is a matter which is of considerable concern to your Honours, I could make further submissions on it as such, but I think that perhaps the issue can be resolved in a different way. I would submit that the mix-up in numbers is understandable, it is a matter of human error. It is unfortunate, certainly there is no question it could have been done better, but I do not think there is any concern that anyone has substituted videos, made them up or anything of that sort. I rely on the fact that in many ways the Austrian police were largely disinterested in the outcome as such, because they knew this case was something that was going to The Hague, it was not their end result, so it seems to me they would have no motive either way. It may be an explanation why not as much care was taken as may have been desirable in the circumstances, but in my submission, that should not affect the admissibility of the documents, because they are quite firm in their evidence that the material seized was in their custody from the time of seizure to the time it was taken to police headquarters, and then it was subsequently recorded and the error was made. It is not the first time these sorts of errors are made in search and seizure operations. They are always difficult matters, but in my submission there is nothing sinister about what happened which would justify an exclusion of the evidence on that basis. However, your Honours, with the first Exhibit I25, I do not know whether your Honours have the extracts of that. This is a video of an interview that took place during 1992 between the witness who appeared here, Divjak, a gentleman of the name Karic, and the accused Zejnil Delalic. There are significant portions of it which relate to the parts where the witness Divjak participates in the interview, and there are parts of it where the witness Delalic speaks on the video in response to questions put to him by a journalist. Your Honours, my colleague Ms McHenry played portions of this video to the witness Divjak, and I will just take your Honours to the transcript where that happens and relate the significant parts of it, which we submit goes to establish its authenticity, reliability and therefore rendering it a document that should be admitted into evidence. At page 8465 of the transcript, at line 7, Ms McHenry says to the witness Divjak: "Sir, I am going to ask you to view an extract from a videotape and ask you if you recognise this as an excerpt of an interview given by you and Mr. Delalic. I would ask the technical people that the excerpt from I25, which is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 115, be shown. After it is shown, I will have a question for you." The excerpt is then played from the videotape, and the transcript of what is said on the videotape is recorded. It was simultaneously translated by the interpreters. The witness then says on page 8467: "If I can just add, I remember that this interview took place between 29th October and 1st or 2nd November, so the situation was quite different from the one that we were discussing, that is the situation in Prozor." Your Honours, in our submission, clearly this witness recognises this tape, this interview that took place and this event. Then there is a further playing of the tape at page 8476, where again Ms McHenry says she wants to play an excerpt of Exhibit 115, tape I25. The video is played and then the witness says -- Ms. McHenry says: "If you can look at it and tell us what is being shown? Answer: International Committee of the Red Cross to the Commander Zejnil Delalic." Then Ms McHenry asks another questions at page 8477 about the Red Cross and its context, but I need not take your Honours through that. In addition, your Honours, this particular -- I am sorry. So, your Honours, in our submission, this videotape not only is a videotape that was located on the premises, and we submit that notwithstanding the error in the counting of it, it nevertheless was corrected by the witnesses Moerbauer and Navrat to the best that they could do so in hindsight. But in addition to that, it has the additional factor of -- indicia of reliability in that it is a video that was recognised and testified to by the witness Divjak. Finally, it is a video which shows the accused Delalic, and although we are only dealing at the moment with the transcript of the video, his appearance on it is also additional evidence of its authenticity and reliability, which we rely on. We say the excerpts that are shown in the transcript that I have provided to your Honours we say is relevant to questions of command responsibilities. It goes to the question of the tension that was existing or developing between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we have heard of in relation to so many of the documents that we have looked at. In those bases, we would say that it is authentic, it is reliable, it is relevant and should properly be admitted into evidence. Your Honours, with the next exhibit, videotape Exhibit 116, and referred to as I46, being a videotape recovered from the premises of INDA-BAU --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt my friend for a moment, my apologies for doing so. There is some confusion in my mind as to how your Honours have dealt with the preliminary issue to which you asked Mr. Niemann to respond, and that is namely to explain the discrepancy. I must ask for clarification at this point and ask where we stand on that particular point which you asked Mr. Niemann to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not what I am about to ask. Which of the tapes come within the next of the exhibits you are trying to tender, which of the tapes, 51 or 54, those tapes as a whole, so we can take them together?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought your Honours had it. I have a copy here, your Honour. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us know how the tapes 51 or 54 are, because they are clearly separate from the first set of tapes, MIB, MIC, MID. They are separate, the INDA-BAU videos, which is not certain whether they are 51 or 54, so we will know what those tapes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is the two tapes that I am now dealing with, Exhibit 115, which is I25 and I46, which is Exhibit 116, they are the two tapes that fall among the 54 tapes that were recovered from the premises of INDA-BAU where the miscounting was taking place, and I have made my submissions about what the state of the evidence is concerning that, namely that the officers says that an error was made and that the error was found some days later. They assert that the tapes were 54 in number originally, that the miscounting must have occurred at the premises of INDA-BAU when the Niederschrift was filled out, but these two tapes fall within that category. They fall within the 54 tapes that were seized at those premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the main contention is if they are 51, the three additional tapes, there must have been three additional tapes. If they are 54 then there are no additional tapes. If we take it as 51, it will not be certain which are the three additional tapes which make them 54. I hope you follow the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand the Defence argument. I am saying that the evidence does not support their argument. The evidence says that there were 54 from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If that is the evidence, the documents would have been consistently 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not if a mistake had been made, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have already indicated, if the Prosecution has indicated 51 on its document when it was seized, now to get to the police headquarters and find 54 appears to be inconsistent with what was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the problem. The mistake is the problem, because if there was a mistake, how do you explain that that mistake did not happen after it was seized?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The state of the evidence is there was a mistake made in the counting, not in the seizure of the videotapes. The state of the evidence from Navrat is that 54 videotapes were seized and the counting of them was the error, not the mistake in the tapes themselves, and that there was not three added. But I have moved to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have. The uncertainty which that mistake has brought into the whole picture, it is what makes it fairly difficult to rely on the fact that they were seized at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honours, but that is why I have presented the evidence on a different basis. If the witness Divjak comes along here and testifies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Divjak can come when the videotape can be viewed. It can only be viewed if you accept it for the purposes of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He viewed it, he has seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter. If finally we discover that these videotapes are tainted with uncertainty, even if he viewed it, perhaps it might give a different picture, it might have been smuggled in after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It could have been, but the chances of that become more remote and fanciful when a witness comes along and says, "Yes, I know about that interview, I participated in it".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He could say so. Then you would still not be arguing that you seized it from the premises of INDA-BAU. You could have brought it after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would not matter where it came from then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But that is not your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But there are two arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then you will not be relying on the fact that you brought it from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is your argument, that you brought it from this place. I have been listening to you carefully, and all the argument is that there are 54 tapes, and if the 54 tapes all come from INDA-BAU, and that is what you rely upon, that it was brought from the premises of the person who is likely to keep them, and they were found from that premises, it is not the same argument as saying that, "I even have the tapes", irrespective of whether it was in that premises. Nothing stops anybody having those tapes. Anybody who was a participant in the exercise could have had that tape and can use it, but when you claim that it was brought from his premises, it is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought I made it clear that my argument was in the alternative. I have alternative arguments. If I have not made that clear, your Honour, I will try and make it clear, but I am presenting to you two arguments. When I started off this morning, I said that not only would I present the transcript of what was said about the miscounting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your alternative argument is that it has been viewed by the General. It was not from the same source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would not matter where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not exclude the fact that it was not from that source, the INDA-BAU tapes which were viewed by the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I could have got it from anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But you did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, your Honour, the alternative argument is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I like forthrightness in arguments and that is why I do not like duplicity of this type. If you had said you got it from INDA-BAU, the tapes, I take it for that. It is possible you got it elsewhere. Now if you are not relying on the INDA-BAU tapes, you could have said so, as the alternative argument that these were not from that collection. It is not your argument that it is not from that collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your Honour suggesting I am not being forthright?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In this argument I have not been satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am very disturbed that you should say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have told you, I have listened to the arguments and you still insist that it was put in the alternative. Your alternative is still the same argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would argue to the contrary on that. I would say that objections to admissibility based on the fact that they were seized from the premises is a matter that troubled your Honours, notwithstanding the fact that I would argue that the evidence would point to the fact that it was just a mistake in counting that was made, but the objection to their admissibility would arise because of their uncertainty in relation to where they came from when they were seized. That would be the objection to their admissibility there. The alternative argument is not affected by that issue, and that is reflected by the fact that Exhibit 114 has already been admitted by your Honours, namely the interview that was conducted with Arif Pasalic, the witness. The reason why your Honours were not concerned about that is because the witness came along and testified to it. The document 114 is also an INDA-BAU tape, I22. It falls into exactly the same category, but it has been accepted into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is a little theoretical. You see, when the evidence is even admitted, if subsequently we find that it is tainted in such a way as to prejudice a fair administration of justice, we can exclude it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not deny your Honour can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is why I want you to establish your arguments so that none of the disqualifying elements affect the evidence which you introduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I need to know, though, whether your Honours do not accept my alternative basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why not? There is no ruling which has been made about it. We will hear the Defence submissions on all the issues before we make up our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is interesting that the Defence themselves have put parts of these videotapes, or parts of the next videotape into evidence themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How does that make everything credible? At the close of the arguments, we will see exactly where everybody stands. That is why we will refrain from making a ruling before all arguments are in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I am troubled that your Honour feels that I am not being forthright, because my intentions were furthest from the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sorry if perhaps I might have said it differently from my intention. My intention is to make it clear that if the argument is based on the fact that these tapes are all from the INDA-BAU premises, it will still be a different concentration from viewing a tape we could have got elsewhere, even though it is the same with the INDA-BAU premises. I agree there might be other copies which could have been brought to be viewed here, but if the argument is that it was not from the premises, then one would not be relying on the collection of 54 which has been stated to have been counted, because it has been the counting that has been the problem. That is the problem, that at least there is a credible counting of 51 and another one of 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it is necessary for me to make it abundantly clear that there is no question from my point of view about where we are saying these documents come from, these videos come from. We say they came from INDA-BAU and at no stage am I suggesting they are coming from anywhere else. What may have occurred is when I said that they could have come from anywhere else, it does not affect the argument, I was merely saying that arguendo to illustrate my point in relation to a witness who comes along before the court and testifies, "yes, I remember this event, I remember when I participated in this event", and what I was merely saying arguendo and by way of illustration is when you have that sort of evidence, that quality of evidence before you, then the issue of whether there was a miscount in the numbers is not a matter that, we would argue, should concern your Honours, because you have first and direct evidence of the witness who says, "yes, this is a video of an event in which I participated". All I was saying is that with the alternative argument, the alternative argument being the person comes along and themselves says, "yes, this is my video", your Honours need not be troubled by the counting. But at no stage was I ever suggesting to your Honours that it may or may not have come from INDA-BAU, I was not putting that to you. My position has always been the same, that our argument is that it came from INDA-BAU and we accept your Honours' concern that you are disturbed by the miscounting, and that may indeed have been fatal, had it not been for the fact that the witnesses admit to the error, and also that somebody else can come along and say that they know of this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you know, the more fatal aspect is that it is not impossible that this tape was not one of those counted. If it was replaced, or if it is an additional tape, if it is 51 and you say, "this is an additional tape".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It becomes mere speculation on my part to suggest where else it would come from. All I know is that on the record, that is not the position that is accepted by the Austrian police. Their position is that there was a miscounting in numbers. Whether that is right or wrong I cannot assist your Honour. That is what they say. The point of reading the transcript was merely to say to your Honours that I do not think bringing them back and questioning them on this point would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It would not make any difference, because they have been closely questioned as to what was in the Niederschrift and what was counted at the police headquarters. That has been established. It was not at the point of seizure of seizure that it was 54, because the forms that are filled at the premises, it was 51 that was filled there, but if the miscounting took place there and not at the police headquarters, then although they have claimed they were in controlling custody possession all through, how many come 54, 3 additional?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the state of the evidence. The state of the evidence is the error was made at the premises of INDA-BAU, when they were originally seized. That is the state of the evidence. That error was not found until later. That is our submission as to the state of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all right. You can continue with the argument, there will be a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a clear misstatement of the facts, that there has been an admission by a police officer that he miscounted on the premises. The record is quite the opposite. That is a clear misstatement of the record and the facts on the record in the testimony of Officer Navrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did not say it was Officer Navrat, your Honours. I rely on page 3740 of the transcript, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think clarity is important. Mr. Navrat never backed off of his Niederschrift where he said there were 51 tapes. He never said in this court, "I made a mistake, I was in a hurry, I did not count them properly", that never happened. Officer Moerbauer was not there. For Officer Moerbauer to say there was apparently a mistake is of no help to your Honours, because he was not there, he was not there when the tapes were counted and counted to be 51. Navrat never came before this court and said, "I made a serious mistake, I was in a hurry, I counted wrong". He stuck by his Niederschrift, he stuck by his 51 number, that is the state of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is another example of one party or another saying, "there is evidence that favours us, so the Trial Chamber has to accept it". As I pointed out earlier in the week, this is something where the Trial Chamber is going to have to make some kind of credibility choice. Just because we have evidence that favours our side, it does not make it wholly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I think when counsel has concluded its argument on it, you will have your right of reply, to make your own points. It is only after that that we will make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, by the allegation of misstatement, no, there is no direct statement by Navrat, but Navrat does say, when confronted with the proposition that three new videotapes were added to the original 51: "Would you accept the possibility, would you not? Answer: Everything is possible, but I have a tough time imagining that." utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would not like to participate in the debate at this stage, but I do wish to say that this method of showing a small segment of a video that we received from the Prosecution, and we do not know where it comes from, and to prove thereby the source of the video I think is inappropriate. We received that insert on at least ten videotapes from the Prosecution, and saying that we saw an insert about the war does still not answer your question where that video comes from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does not, but if the Defence use it for the purposes of questioning a witness or impeaching a witness or whatever, then it suggests that they themselves must place some credibility on the document or videotape, otherwise they would be doing nothing other than, I would submit, misleading the Chamber, which I am sure they would not do. It is significant that they relied on it for the limited purposes that they did. Also the same video, a portion of the same video was shown to the witness Branko Gotovac in the course of cross-examination of that witness by Ms McMurrey. Your Honours, that is not the only basis upon which we argue in the alternative. I keep emphasising now that it is in the alternative. We are not suggesting that it came from anywhere other than INDA-BAU. Your Honours, during the course of the record of interview with the accused Zejnil Delalic, at page 3 of the record of interview, he is questioned by the investigator in relation to an interview that he gave at a Zagreb TV programme called, "Slikom na Sliku", and I have taken your Honours to this previously in relation to another matter, namely whether he was in Zagreb in early May, but it is this programme that appears as part of I46, Exhibit 116. Do your Honours have the copy of that in front of you? I hand a copy up to your Honours. (Handed). It is quite a long interview, but we have only extracted the limited parts that we are seeking to rely on. It is composed of two components, it is this interview on the programme "Slikom na Sliku", but there is another part of it which is entitled "the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina", which is again part of this long video. I think it runs for something in the area of three hours, so we have only extracted a very short part of it for the purposes of the Prosecution case. The point that I wish to make now is that this video is about that interview in Zagreb in May when the accused Zejnil Delalic was interviewed, and it shows him participating in the interview. He is questioned about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When he was a co-ordinator, or before his appointment as co-ordinator? I think co-ordinator appointment is 12th May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The evidence is not clear on that. It is possibly before he was appointed co-ordinator. He was certainly active in Konjic at the time establishing the fledgling army, but the point I wish to make in connection with the interview is he was asked by the investigators whether he was interviewed on this programme, he says yes, and then the question is: "When was that? Answer: That was in the month of May when I went to Zagreb for logistics. Question: Beginning of May, mid May, end of May? Answer: First half of May. Question: What was the purpose of the interview? Answer: There was an association of people from Konjic and Zagreb. The war had only just begun, and they wanted to hear about more what was happening in Konjic. You know that Konjic is 350 kilometres away. Since it was the beginning of the war, they wanted to have accurate information on what was happening in Herzegovina and what kind of co-operation existed between the TO and the HVO. Question: How come you were selected for interview?" He explains he happened to be coming from the area. The point that I wish to raise by this point is that there is nothing that emerges from the record of interview to suggest that this interview did not take place as a matter of fact and that he did not participate in it. As I said, your Honours, the tape is a very long tape, and there is a large section on it entitled, "The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina". The investigators go on at page 5 of the record of interview of 23rd August 1996, and they say in relation to the balance of this particular videotape, which was the part that dealt with the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they say: "Was this the same journalist as in another context had told you that you were the leader when the Celebici barracks were liberated?" It is on page 5, your Honours. The accused says: "I do not understand, what other context? Question: Because from one of the videotapes we seized in Vienna on 18th March this year, 1996, there is a sequence where you are told to be the leader of the group that liberated Celebici barracks and you were the person who organised the prison in the military barracks in Celebici." Then the investigator says: "This is told by a journalist in the video we seized, a video called, 'War of Bosnia-Herzegovina'." That is the title given. The accused then says: "My question to you is whether this videotape in the sequence is not just a commentary that is taped or recorded in between the footage, or the broadcast live, or directly recorded." The investigator said: "This is a videotape that consists of several clips from TV. My question is just to find out whether it is just one journalist who claimed you, all the time, who bragged to you to be leader of the area at the time, or are there more than one journalist who made that kind of statement that you were most important leader in Konjic area at the time, April/May." The accused says in relation to that aspect of the matter: "The videotape to which you are referring was made one year later in Vienna." I need to just clarify this here. Your Honours appreciate, there are two parts of the video. There is the part that was recorded from the television series in Zagreb in May 1992, and there is another feature part of the video which is a much bigger part and it is entitled, "The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina". That is the part which he is referring to now, that he is talking about. He says: "The videotape to which you are referring was made one year later in Vienna and all the comments I give on these films in between footages are invented and you can just forget about it. Those comments were made by amateurs in a Bosnian club in Vienna." I emphasise at this point we are not seeking to tender any of those parts of the video. He has said that they were exaggerated and we do not know to the contrary. Besides, the only part of the videotapes that we are interested in are the parts where he the accused is himself speaking, we are not seeking to get into evidence commentary by journalists or whatever about the matter, and so in the extracts we have provided to your Honours we have been careful to exclude those parts which are not speaking parts by the accused. The investigator then goes on, further down the page: "Who made the video, 'The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina'? Answer: The footage, they came from different sources, from all over, some people private video, something that was recorded from the TV, but the comments that you can hear on the videotape are made by a kind of cultural section of the Bosnian Culture Club in Vienna." Your Honours, nowhere when questioned about this matter does the accused say, "well, if you received that from premises in Vienna, that was a mistake", or, "that was never there, you got that wrong". Nowhere does he ever say, "you people must have fabricated this", or, "the Vienna police must have fabricated this, because I do not know anything about it", which one would expect him to say if that is the case. What he says is what one would expect him to say. He says yes, that he knows of it, that he acknowledges that the first part or the part that relates to the interview in Zagreb in May 1992, that is correct, and he explains his participation in that. But what he says is that with the part of the tape that relates to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina that there are components in that which were made by journalists and others, and he says they are not accurate. We are not seeking to tender those, your Honours. Your Honours, in our submission, you have before you in relation to this videotape the very best evidence that you could possibly have, the very best evidence, because it comes from the accused himself, and at no stage does he attempt to say to your Honours that it is something which was not at the premises or it was something that must have been made up by the Prosecution or the Vienna police or by somebody else who had such malicious intent. We submit, your Honour, that this video, extracts of the video we have provided your Honours with, is admissible and relevant. We say that the first part, segment 1, is relevant because it speaks of what the accused was doing in those very early parts of the war in May 1992, being interviewed on Zagreb Television. It speaks of the barracks at Celebici being recovered, it refers to an ultimatum which was issued to the JNA, in which the accused himself had some role, and is referred to in the record of interview. It refers to the joint command between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which your Honours have heard so much about in the course of the evidence. The video also contains that segment that I referred your Honours to previously, where the use of the call name, "Oganj", meaning "fire", is also contained as part of this extract of the video. On all of those bases, if your Honours please, we submit that because the accused himself has made reference to this video, has not contested its existence, that it is relevant, that it is authentic and it should properly be admitted into evidence. Those are our submissions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before my learned friend sits down, could I just ask him to deal with one thing that he has literally just mentioned, and that is in segment 8, bottom two lines of that segment. utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is not what it says, it just says "Oganj", of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in connection with this discussion, I should just like to draw attention to a point which should not mislead us. It is true that during the interview with Mr. Delalic, certain subjects were discussed. I must say that the Prosecution submitted to us 80 and more tapes, some from entertainment, others dealing with the questions of the war. utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the videotape contains two segments, as I thought I had explained, the segment relating to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina segment, and the other part which related to the programme on the Zagreb TV, "Slikom na Sliku". The tape was mentioned on page 5 of the transcript in relation to that part of the tape pertaining to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the investigator says: "Because one of the videotapes we seized in Vienna on 18th March this year, 1996, there was a sequence in which you were", and then he continues questioning, so there is no question that at least the second part of the tape, that was raised directly with the accused during the course of his record of interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you rightly said, Vienna is a big city. It was clearly stated that this cassette is from INDA-BAU. The interview conducted with my client does not affect the reliability of this video. There is a legitimate way for the Prosecution to authenticate every segment. utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is not inconsistent with the ways, matters, documents and material presented before other trial chambers in relation to other matters, so I do not know to what my friend is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour Judge Jan asked me to clear up a couple of matters in relation to the last video exhibit that I have dealt with, exhibit P116 and in particular that part in segment 10. Your Honours, it was discussed with the accused in the record of interview of 18th and 19th March 1996, at page 51 and 52, and again at page 55. Certainly he agrees that he took part in the interview, but he said that he was not there at the same time as the filming that took place, so it looks as though there was filming at the camp, he went to the camp, but then the filming segment that he participated in, according to his version of it, was back at his house. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we are at Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, may it please you. This is plainly an important issue, given the amount of time which we have dedicated to this particular matter. I want, with your Honours' indulgence this afternoon, to address to you some rather more general remarks about the nature of the exercise that the Prosecution invites you to conduct when admitting these documents. In so doing, I hope to remind you, of course you probably do not need reminding, but I am going to do so whether you like it or not, of some fundamental matters of law, something which so far has been missing from the address of the Prosecution. Some time ago in the summer, when there was sun and it was still shining and warm, there was a motion filed on the issue of cross-examination. It was an issue which was dealt with by both written and oral argument. Quite apart from the well argued debate on both sides, there was, we say, a particularly revealing aspect of that argument on that occasion which has now surfaced again. We say this: the argument on that occasion demonstrated that the reality is that the Prosecution did not care greatly for the way in which cross-examination was being conducted. It may well be that they had worked out that their witnesses were not faring terribly well under the process of scrutiny that cross-examination necessarily involves. Indeed your Honours may recall during the course of the argument that took place that the Prosecution evinced a distaste for cross-examination by surprise. You may recall that I had to remind your Honours that I thought all cross-examination was supposed to be a surprise. In due course, your Honours gave your views about cross-examination, and those rules that you set out for us have, I hope, been applied universally by us. Because of the way in which argument has been put forward by my learned friend Mr. Niemann on this occasion, I respectfully submit to you that the Prosecution did not take such reverse, as they felt, lying down. What we say is that this exercise that you are being invited to conduct is demonstration of how they think they can get evidence in front of you without the process of cross-examination taking place. This is not peripheral evidence. They say it is central to their case. They say this is evidence which will assist you to convict the defendants, so from that point of view, this is highly important evidence. When you think of how important they say it is, and you look at the casual way that you are invited to take it and admit it, you will see that the process that is involved is both one that is very important, and we say the way in which they are inviting you to do it is in fact thoroughly unjust. What they are doing is presenting you with a process which involves them in not having to go through the inconvenience of calling people, and I am going to give you a specific example, the inconvenience of calling someone who could give evidence about these documents and the events set out in them, without the inconvenience of that person being called and being cross-examined, and the evidence being shown to be thoroughly untrustworthy and unreliable. What we say is this: this exercise, and the manner in which you are invited to admit these documents, is one which would simply drive a coach and horses through some fundamental rights which are guaranteed to each of the defendants in this case, clear rights guaranteed by the Articles of the Statute and reinforced by Rules of Evidence. I am going to come in due course to two articles, Article 20 and Article 21, and two rules, Rule 89 and Rule 95. Let me first of all identify to your Honours three types of document which are involved in this process. Firstly, there are documents which purport to be written by somebody who is not a party to these proceedings, and who has not been called as a witness. Secondly, there are documents which are wholly unsigned and which are not capable of attribution to anybody. Thirdly, there are documents which purport to be written by a defendant. In respect of this part of the argument, I intend only to deal with the first and third categories, and in the light of the law that I am going to recite to you, I am going to make the following propositions in relation to those documents. In the respect of the first class of documents, that is documents that purport to be the work of someone who is not a defendant, who is not a party and who has not been called to give evidence. Let us just consider for a moment what is the nature of the information which is set out in such a document. It is an account of events and personalities that are said to have taken place in Bosnia in 1992. In the sense that it is such an account of such events, it is effectively just like a piece of hearsay evidence which comes from the witness box, with a number of important distinctions. The first obvious distinction is this: there is no witness actually recounting the events to you. You never get to see and hear the witness, and thus assess his demeanour and truthfulness. As importantly, the defendant never gets to see and hear that witness, hear his evidence and hear him being challenged. The declarant in the document is not subject to cross-examination to test the veracity of what he has set out allegedly in that document. So it comes to this: the facts which are alleged and set out in the document are not subject to any form of critical scrutiny, and most importantly, we have no way whatever of testing the accuracy, reliability and truthworthiness of the declarant in the document. We respectfully submit that admitting such documents would amount to a clear and unambiguous breach of the two Articles of the Statute that I have mentioned, and by reasons of Rule 89D and Rule 95, your Honours ought not to admit them. Let me please, and forgive me for taking some time to do this, but it is important, remind your Honours of the law. First of all, Article 20(1). The headnote of that Article refers to the conduct of trial proceedings. It says this: "The Trial Chambers shall ensure that a trial is fair and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with full respect for the rights of the accused." Your Honours will notice that the terms of that Article are mandatory and the phraseology that is used is, "shall ensure", and so there is no ambiguity about the requirement that is laid upon your Honours' shoulders to carry out that duty. If I may turn now to Article 21(2): "In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing, subject to Article 22", which as your Honours will recall concerns protection of victims and witnesses. Article 21(4): "In the determination of any charge against the accused, pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality." Subparagraph E of that, one of those is to examine or have examined the witnesses against him; as I say, the terminology is mandatory. It requires your Honours to carry out those duties. Here is the neat trick that we say the Prosecution is inviting you to take on board: by getting you to admit these documents, they put before you someone's account which can never be tested by cross-examination, and can never be challenged in any way at all. After all, you cannot cross-examine a document, can you? We respectfully submit that this breaches the requirement in Article 21(4)E, which entitles defendants to examine or have examined the witnesses against him. It is an account that is given and placed before you which is not subject to any form of critical scrutiny. The effect of allowing these documents in would be to deprive each accused of that right which is guaranteed to him to cross-examine the declarant of evidence about him. We respectfully submit that this demonstrates the inherent unfairness and unjustness of the exercise that you are being invited to conduct. If one needed any reinforcement in that view, one only has to look at the terminology of Rule 89 and Rule 95. Rule 89B: "A Chamber shall apply Rules of Evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law." We respectfully submit that the rules in relation to the proof of documents should be rules which are consonant with the spirit of the Statute, and the Statute makes it quite plain that if there is someone who gives an account, there has to be a right to cross-examine. If that right is taken away, then the rules cannot be said to be consonant with the spirit of the Statute. Rule 89C, of course, your Honours are familiar with, the admission of relevant evidence which is deemed to have probative value. Rule 89D: "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a need to ensure a fair trial." The latter part of that sentence plainly reflects the duties that are laid upon the Tribunal in Articles 20 and 21. Rule 89E, of course, entitling your Honours to request verification of authenticity of evidence obtained out of court. This is evidence which on the face of it is obtained out of court and I remind your Honour of that power that you have. It is not put there as an idle makeweight to make the Rule look a bit better, it is there for a fundamental purpose, to ensure that when issues of authenticity are raised, your Honours have a clear power to make the Prosecution, and indeed the Defence for that matter, demonstrate authenticity. Rule 95. This rule is phrased in a mandatory way as well, in strong terms: "No evidence shall be admissible if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." We respectfully submit that taking those Rules together with the Articles of the Statute, that lays a ground for saying this: there must be proper rules for the admissibility of documents. First of all, authentication, reliability, and then and only then can the court move on to the stage of deciding relevance and probative value. Your Honour, the same can be said with a slight distinction to the third class of documents to which I adverted. Those are documents which purport, and for reasons I come to in due course will say to you that we do not for a moment accept that there is a scrap of evidence that any document in this case, subject to this application by the Prosecution, has been proved to be a document of a defendant, but let us assume for the sake of this argument that it is a document of the defendant. A similar argument applies. I am not going to go through the Rules and the Statute again, but, of course, I remind your Honours of Article 21G, which says that a defendant cannot be compelled to testify. The effect of that, of course, is this, and there is a glaring example here. Admitting this document allows the -- admitting document 130, for example, allows the Prosecution to get in an account by a defendant which is not subject to cross-examination. We respectfully submit that there is a clear breach in that process of the Articles to which I have adverted, because of the operation of Rule 89D and 95 ought plainly to be excluded. We come back to where I have started. I respectfully submit to you that is the process of how the Prosecution are getting in front of people material which is wholly untested and incapable of being tested. You cannot cross-examine a document. I come now to the specific example which shows quite clearly what the Prosecution are trying to do. You will recall from some of the documents that have been placed before you the name "Esad Ramic". His name appears quite frequently in those documents. You may have other reasons to recall Esad Ramic. We say that the case of Esad Ramic demonstrates beyond a peradventure that what the Prosecution is trying to do is stifle cross-examination, trying to deprive the defendants of their rights. You do not need to go very far to find the numerous references to Mr. Ramic, and references to events in which Mr. Ramic was plainly said to be involved, and which Mr. Ramic might be expected to remember and have knowledge of. Let me take you back a couple of weeks or so. Your Honours will recall an application, a motion before this court, a motion for the issuance of a subpoena against Mr. Ramic, who was said to be unwilling to attend this court. He came to The Hague once your Honours had issued that subpoena. We do not know, because he never gave evidence, whether he, like others, had in fact been willing all along and that the information given to my learned friends was incorrect as well, but he was here, he was behind that door somewhere. He was available. He could have been called by the Prosecution, and asked about those matters which are referred to in these documents. He could have given evidence, he could have authenticated the events in those documents. He was ready to give evidence. What did the Prosecution do? They said they could do without him, they could do without his evidence, and so they sent him home. No evidence-in-chief, no cross-examination. They sent him home, because they could do without his evidence. I bet they could do without his evidence. We respectfully submit that that is a clear indication of the way in which they could in fact prove these documents and the fact that they are reluctant to do it in that way at all. There is a much easier way for them, just put them in front of your Honours and say they are authentic. That way nobody can test the truth of what is in the documents. Your Honour, I make some general points in furtherance of my argument about the nature of many of these. First of all, documents which are by someone who is not a party or a witness. In almost every case, there is no proof whatever that in fact the document is genuine. There is no proof whatever that in fact it is by the person whose name is said to be on the bottom of the document. There is no proof whatever of any of those things. In relation to documents whose author is unclear, there is no evidence of authorship, so one cannot even begin to say in relation to those documents if there is any degree of reliability to them. It is impossible to demonstrate anything like accuracy, reliability and truthworthiness, which we respectfully submit are the criteria that your Honours should apply. Documents purporting to be written by individual defendants; there simply is not a shred of proof that any document was in fact written by a defendant. Let me give you a plain example of the dangers, the fallacy that is being proposed to you. There are documents which are said to have been written by Mr. Delalic. They are said to be written by him because his nickname, his code-word was "Oganj". Your Honours know that in fact there were two people using the code-word "Oganj", because it is there in the record of the video. Of course the Prosecution are going to say, "we say it refers to Mr. Delalic when it is at the bottom of the document". Their problem is that there are two people using the same code-word, and it could equally be, because there is no evidence about it, it could equally be the other man who is using the code-word "Oganj" too. Your Honour, that, we respectfully say, demonstrates the great dangers that are involved in following what may seem at first blush an attractive proposition by my learned friend; but when you look at it, look at an example like that, there lies the danger, that you are just asked by my learned friend to simply take these documents on trust. That is what he is doing. No proof, no authenticity, no reliability; "just trust us", say the Prosecution. We respectfully submit that if you allege that some document was written by a defendant, and that it can be used against that defendant, there are no two ways about it: it is incumbent on the person so asserting to prove that that document was created by that defendant. If you do not do so, then it should not be admitted, because it has no indication of reliability whatever. There are, of course, many ways in which documents can be proved. One of them has been referred to in this court, by showing them to a defendant in interview and getting him to admit that is his document. It has not been done, save in two innocuous examples in this case. I am not going to go through a list of the ways in which you can properly and very simply prove documents, but there is one example of how you would do it. They did not bother to do that at interview, and now when it comes to actually doing the job properly, they try and put this Heath Robinson affair together, a skimpy way of getting you to admit it by saying, "we say it is authentic and therefore it is okay". Let me just come to this. This is what the Prosecution are inviting you to do. They say, "here is a document". They say, "it bears the name of", for example, "Mucic". They say, "it is therefore without any further evidence demonstrated to be Mucic's document". That is a very dangerous process. The Prosecution's approach to proof of documents, we say, is wholly cavalier. The approach appears to be there: your Honours are professional judges. We can put any document in front of you we like. When we do that, we submit to you the document is true and was written by the person it purports to have been written by. We do not need to prove anything else and all you have to decide is the weight to attach to it. The fact that it is a forgery matters not; if we say it is reliable, that ought to be enough, and if there is some challenge to authenticity of the documents, all that needs to happen is counsel for the Prosecution has to give evidence, he says, "it is a document which has the appearance of a genuine document", just like the ones you have already been looking at. There, they say, "you have all the authenticity you need". That, we submit, is the process of admitting documents, the process the Prosecution invites you to employ. Can I just give you, it may sound like an absurd example, but it may help to illustrate what the process is in a light-hearted way, one which I think will draw your Honours' attention to what is really involved. It is at this point that I am going to make fun of Mr. Moran. I am sure he does not mind that, but just follow me if you will. Let us assume for a moment that my learned friend Mr. Moran suddenly becomes suspected of being a Texan, which, of course, as your Honour knows is a very serious offence. As a result of that, a search warrant is obtained to permit his office here in The Hague and other premises to be raided and searched. In accordance with that search warrant, an elite squad of the Vienna police is assembled and they go in and raid his room here in the Tribunal. It is an office to which many have access. On the desk is a document. It is seized along with many other documents. That main document is signed "T Moran" and it bears an official looking stamp, which no doubt says the word "Texas" somewhere on it. The main document contains a number of statements and they are these: "Texas is a small island in the south Pacific"; "there are no cowboys wearing silly hats in Texas"; "Texas was discovered in 1350 by an obscure Italian explorer who was very lost. When he got home he said to his fellow adventurers 'I now know what Dante was getting at when he wrote “The Inferno." Those are plainly absurd statements. Amongst the many other documents which are recovered are a number which refer to Mexico. When the court case comes up and we put Mr. Moran on trial for being a Texan, we place before the court the main document and all the other documents which mention Mexico, and then we make these assertions: "the main document bears his signature, we have no evidence whatever that this is so, but you must take this as an undisputed fact. The stamp on it looks like the other ones we have been looking at in the case and it has the appearance of being genuine. Therefore you must take it that it is genuine. There is a thread running through the document, it is all about Texas. There is also a thread running through the other documents, it is all about Mexico. Of course, Mexico is very near Texas, is it not? These threads mean Mr. Moran is a Texan and he is guilty of the offence, even though we have no proof whatever that it is his document". Taking all those facts together, the court can say not only is it authentic and genuine but it is both relevant and probative and Mr. Moran is proved to be, as we said, a Texan. In fact, the document was really written by Mr. Ackerman, who planted it on his desk with a view to damaging his reputation as a well-educated, debonair man. That is the exercise that you are being invited to do in this case, your Honours. Absolutely that, putting 2 and 2 together and ending up with 5. Your Honour, we respectfully submit this: this is a good opportunity for your Honours to lay down a set of rules, rules comparable to the decision in the Tadic case involving hearsay; rules which will stand this Tribunal in good stead and will set a benchmark for the way in which documents can properly be admitted, using those features that I have adverted to in so doing. I know through having discussed it with him that my learned friend Mr. Ackerman has a formulation which he would wish to suggest to your Honours, because, of course, this is a matter of general importance, not just to the defendants Mucic and Delalic, but to all defendants, not just in this trial but to others as well. What we say is that your Honours should reject what is an unjust and unworthy system which you are invited to take on board by the Prosecution. Your Honours will be relieved to know that I am not going to take you through document after document, line by line. I am not going to do that. I am simply going to pick one example in order to illustrate that which I have been saying. It is document 130. The Prosecution make great play of this document. The reality is that there is no evidence whatever that that document was created by Zdravko Mucic. There is no evidence that it is a genuine Bosnian Consulate document. There is a perfectly simple way to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The consul is not Republic, or is he a counsel, or is he a diplomatic officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: A consul is entitled to the protections of the relevant convention that deal with diplomats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just wondering whether the consul in this document, is he just equivalent to Republic and not to anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have not a clue, and I am not going to give evidence, your Honour. It is undated, and I think that was something that your Honour Judge Jan pointed out, that there is no date on this document. If it is a genuine document, that is rather curious, civil servants, of course, being notorious for putting dates on things. This document could have been created at any time or by anybody, and here is an important fact, it is addressed to the 4th Corps at Mostar. You have heard about the 4th Corps at Mostar. General Pasalic knows a little bit about the 4th Corps at Mostar. He could have been asked about this document and he was not. Of course, there is a contrast here with the custodian of records, Mr. Omerkic. Your Honours, I am told we are due to have another custodian of records this afternoon. The contrast between the process of calling a custodian of records and shoving a load of documents in front of you you may think is rather noteworthy. The document was not found in Mr. Mucic's possession. He was never asked about it in interview and he could have been. Those are points which apply to pretty well every document, with perhaps a couple of exceptions in this case. There were some, of course, which Mr. Delalic was invited to examine and admit. By themselves, they are pretty innocuous, but these are comments that we say apply pretty well equally across the board. There is not a scrap of evidence of authenticity and reliability. We say the whole exercise is flawed, Prosecution has not even bothered to try and suggest that they are authenticating these in anything like a proper manner. Well, that is pretty well all I have to say. There is one final thing concerning the videos. If you think they help the Prosecution, of course that is a matter for you. We submit they are of absolutely zero relevance and zero probative value and if they do have any of those qualities, they have precious little weight. The Prosecution wants to play pictures of Zara Mrkajic, plump and well fed, a prisoner in the camp; that is their affair. We say they are of precious little assistance in this case. Your Honour, those are my submissions. We respectfully invite you to reject this process. It is an unjust one, it is unfair, and the case of Mr. Ramic demonstrates that absolutely and clearly. We say that is how they should have done it, they ducked it. It is an unjust way in which they are inviting you to deal with these documents. I invite you to say, "we are going to resist that, we are going to set a proper and necessarily high standard for the admissibility of documents and leave this Tribunal a sound basis which others can follow for the admissibility of documents in a proper and disciplined way". Thank you very much, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the leave of your Honours, I will just address you from here, because I expect to be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. When I began to think about these documents, about three things came to mind. The first of those, of course, being an advocate, was the interests of my client. But to a great extent, this issue goes significantly beyond that. The law has always been a very important thing to me, something that I have learnt to love throughout my career, and my career has taken me to a lot of different places in that, including a place very similar to where your Honours are sitting this afternoon. For there to be a rule of law, there must be a public respect for law. That is what makes the rule of law possible. As I then began to think about that, I began to think about what the role of your Honours is with regard to this issue and the role of this Tribunal. The Tribunal, of course, needs to be seen by the world as a place where fair trials can be had. Your fellow judges on this Tribunal in handling future cases are entitled to the wisdom and guidance of you original judges from this Tribunal as they approach the work that they will have to do here. One deficiency that I think is clear as you look at the decisions of this Tribunal so far is a clear and comprehensive decision regarding how this Tribunal should handle documentary evidence. Documentary evidence is a very complicated and difficult evidence issue, one which courts across the world have dealt with for centuries in different ways, and it is an issue which has evolved as our society has become more and more dependent upon paper and communication through the use of paper, and now we are approaching the electronic age and in the electronic age, where all sorts of questions regarding computer records and things of that nature are becoming important, in terms of documentary evidence. I think this Trial Chamber should be willing and is certainly capable to take some time and to draft for your fellow judges and the future judges here, and for notice of the world community, a comprehensive set of rules by which you can arrive at a decision about the documents that are before you today. It is something you will necessarily have to do for yourselves in going through this process, in any event. I would hope that you would decide to share it with your fellow judges and future judges. I know from my own experience that one of the great enemies of a judge is expediency. You tend to be sitting on a particular case and become so wrapped up in that particular case that expediency begins to take on an importance that it never deserves, but the temptation is always there, and it is one that we must all resist. Even in the lowest court, when a judge speaks of the law, the judge always speaks beyond the case before him, always speaks beyond the case before him, and when you speak of the law in this case, you are speaking beyond the Celebici case. You are speaking to your fellow judges, you are speaking to history, because in an International Tribunal, we all must recognise what we do here as having historical significance. We sit here 50 years later and we can read what those judges at Nuremberg and those judges at Tokyo did and wrote and said, because it is important and it is published and it is available. Some of those decisions and pronouncements look pretty good 50 years later; some of them do not stand the light very well at all. When we talk about documentary evidence, pieces of paper sought to be introduced in a case as evidence in the case, we are virtually in every case speaking of evidence that is hearsay. They contain out of court statements offered for the proof of their contents. That is the classic definition of hearsay. So you always begin, in my mind, an analysis of documentary evidence with that view, the document that is being offered before you is hearsay. One of the things about hearsay evidence, and the reason that the law is so careful about admitted hearsay evidence, is the understanding that it cannot be cross-examined, and with that understanding, the statements of the declarant contained in those documents must have such circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness that the court can say cross-examination would not affect it in any way. It is so golden as it stands that cross-examination is not necessary. These documents, I submit, your Honours, need to be viewed in exactly that light, so the first task that you must perform is you look at them as hearsay, which is what they are, and determine whether there are circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness that would make cross-examination a futile exercise. If you find that there are not, then your inquiry ends at that point. There is no need to go beyond there. If you find those circumstantial guarantees of truthworthiness do exist, then you must go next, I suggest, to the question of authenticity. I think authenticity is sometimes difficult in application but rather simple in understanding.
