A document is authentic if it is what the proponent of that document says it is; in other words, if I hand you a piece of paper and say, "this is the front page of today's New York Herald Tribune -- International Herald Tribune", if there is proof it is what I say it is, then it is an authentic document. If I hand you a piece of paper found on Mr. Moran's desk which contains what appears to be his signature and say to you "your Honours, this is a letter written by Mr. Moran", by that I have not authenticated that document, I would have to go beyond that, I would have to find a witness that watched him sign it, I would have to find an expert that could compare the handwriting, I would have to find some other evidence that I could present to you to make that document authentic. If, as you look at each of the documents in this case, you must conclude that the Prosecutor has failed beyond a reasonable doubt to prove to you that the document is authentic, then that is where your inquiry ends. It does not go beyond there. If on the other hand you find that there is proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the document being offered to you is authentic, then you must perform a third and final analysis. That third and final analysis has to do with the concept of relevancy and probative value. The question that you ask yourselves in that case is, "do the statements contained in the document tend to make an issue contained within the indictment in the case that needs to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt either more probable or less probable?". If it does, then it has relevance and probative value; if it does not, then again your inquiry ends and the document is not admitted. It seems to me that the process I have just described is one that in one form or another any judge must go through in terms of deciding on whether or not documentary evidence is admitted into a case. I would hope, and I would strongly suggest to your Honours, that you apply that kind of an analysis to these documents, but also take some time to express your wisdom in that regard in writing so that future tribunals, future prosecutors, future defence lawyers will have a guide to help them prepare their cases. Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other contributions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have been participating in this very important difficult trial, which is being watched by the world, since 10th March, and all people interested in justice are watching us, whether we are correctly establishing the facts, whether we are contributing to the development of law and justice. My distinguished colleagues have drawn your attention to the provisions of the Statute, Articles 20 and 21, and I must say with satisfaction that taking part in these proceedings until quite recently as an attorney, the Defence counsel of my client, Mr. Delalic, I was absolutely satisfied in the way in which this Trial Chamber has been conducting the proceedings and seeking to ensure and protect the rights of all the accused, including my client. However, this week we have been confronted with a very difficult task that my learned colleagues have drawn the attention of the Trial Chamber to with abundant arguments. As the Defence counsel of Mr. Delalic, for which the Prosecutor is offering evidence claiming that it is relevant, in a method which is inappropriate to the proceedings so far and it puts us in a very difficult position. Submitting one document after another, the authenticity of which was not proven in any way, whose probative value was not proven, a document for which my client could not cross-examine the witness and implement his rights guaranteed by Article 21, we almost accepted this procedure, and responded to each of the documents. We have a large number of documents before us. We are ready, if you consider that to be the appropriate procedure, that is the kind suggested by the Prosecution, rather than the one described by my colleagues, we are ready to argue each individual document, but not in the way the Prosecutor is suggesting; that is to compare an unauthentic text with highly doubtful value with another unauthenticated text of a similar value, but rather by grouping some of those documents to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the extent to which they are not authentic and how problematic their reliability is and what little value they have, and which does not compare at all well with what we have been doing ever since 10th March. Since we have before us a considerable number of documents, which we would refer to if that is your decision, in that case, I would ask that my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, and myself could share and divide between us our arguments. We would be forced to analyse the documents in a way which we do not consider to be appropriate, but if that is in the interests of our client, we will do that. Before you give us instructions as to the way in which we should proceed, I should like to draw your attention to two points only. Within the series of documents that my learned colleague Mr. Niemann has led us through very skilfully, we heard many facts about the war, we heard many facts about Mr. Delalic, we learned about other facts conveyed by hearsay without any possibility of checking what was said. Forgive me for reminding you of something, which I do not like an attorney to do, because I objected when this was done by my colleague Mr. Niemann. Your Honours, I was in the war for four years, I spent four years in a city under siege, and every day I experienced thousands of facts brought by war, weapons and shooting and wounding and the exile of my own children, and during those four years, we never shed any tears. A few days ago I saw a wonderful film by Ademir Kenovic, awarded in Cannes. That film put into two hours many facts from the lives of us, 300,000 inhabitants of Sarajevo. Not one of those was truthful, but it reflected some of the truth of the war, and we as spectators were crying. Therefore telling us the stories of many people who lived in Konjic, who fled from Konjic, who came to clubs in Austria, Germany and elsewhere and recounted in their own words about something that happened or may not have happened, that story that we heard in the past few days is not one that I am prepared to eliminate using the same procedure. Something else that perhaps may not be also absolutely appropriate, but Judge Jan drew attention to it, saying that in the course of the war, criminal proceedings were instituted against some of the defendants here. I know that you are not bound by national legislation, but I would like to indicate to your Honours that according to our law, criminal charges are just charges. They are not any condemnation. They are studied by the investigating magistrate and only then is a decision taken to remove any doubts. Therefore, according to our laws, which are quite different from those here, the accused and their relatives cannot testify, and they are not bound to tell the truth. Many of the documents referred to by the Prosecutor may be indicative of a period in which the defendants, the accused, the family or relatives participated in some such proceedings may have written something that may or may not be correct. The Prosecutor has not even tried to prove the reliability of any of those facts or those sources. Therefore, completing this part of my objection before going on to an analysis of each of the individual documents, I wish to say once again that we fully endorse what has been said by colleagues Greaves and Ackerman, so we would like your Honours to give us instructions as to how we should proceed from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is a real surprise to me. What I expected you to do was to answer the submissions of the Prosecutor. If you have any shortfalls in them, if you have any criticisms of them, you make them. It is not for me to direct you differently from what has been happening within the Trial Chamber. I thought that was the normal method and that might determine the Trial Chamber's approach.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. My colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, if you allow it, and in view of the large number of objections that we will have, he will be the first to make them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are free to argue your case whichever way you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. My submissions will be relatively short and with your indulgence I will make them from here. First of all, I will begin by saying that on behalf of Mr. Delalic we adopt in toto previous submissions made by Mr. Greaves and Mr. Ackerman. I will begin myself with a general observation referring first to your decision of 12th September, where you ruled that the chain of custody of the folders had been proven, but not the contents of those folders. As we have heard so far, proving the authenticity of these documents is the first and fundamental link and step in proving these documents and determining their admissibility. I would like to remind your Honours of what the record clearly states. My friend Mr. Niemann has said that according to Mr. Moerbauer's testimony he was handed folders by his colleague, Navrat, but the contents of those folders were not analysed, according to Mr. Moerbauer, until 22nd March through 2nd April, when he marked those documents in Vienna, and when he came to this Tribunal he could not identify his mark on any of the documents. Officer Moerbauer was called specifically -- for the specific purpose of identifying those documents. Any suggestion, as my learned friend Mr. Niemann has put before you, that Officer Moerbauer adopted a new numbering system at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor is not borne out by his testimony or the facts. If I might briefly address you now on the issue of videos, three videos in particular, the three allegedly from INDA-BAU. This morning, my friend Mr. Niemann said that the discrepancy of three videos between the 51 and the 54 could be explained easily by the fact that they were miscounted. Might I remind your Honours that the record is quite clear. The witness Navrat was led through examination-in-chief by Mr. Niemann on 5th August. Officer Navrat, in Exhibit 165, a Niederschrift, clearly testified to the fact that he seized 51 videos, page 5644, his hand-written Niederschrift attests to that. Mr. Niemann never doubted or questioned Mr. Navrat to ask him if that was a correct number or not. Mr. Navrat stood by that number. In fact the only thing Mr. Niemann questioned Mr. Navrat about was the correctness of the date on the Niederschrift, to which Mr. Navrat admitted there was an error. Therefore there was no questioning of Navrat to ask him to acknowledge that the number of 51 videotapes was incorrect. Mr. Navrat in cross-examination confirmed that the operation was well manned, there was no pressure, there was no hurry, there were no complaints and no incidents. Mr. Navrat's report of 18th March again confirms that there were 51 videotapes seized. The second relevant point in the testimony of Officer Panzer, again led by Mr. Niemann on direct examination on 2nd September, shows that in the report prepared by Panzer, 22nd April, there are 54 videotapes, 54 videotapes which according to Panzer he marked on 19th and 20th March, and the first indication that there is a discrepancy in numbers is this report of 22nd April 1996. It is clear therefore that there is a discrepancy of three videos, but any suggestion there is an error in counting is not borne out by the facts. Might I remind your Honours of the transcript at page 3779; if I go back to that date, that is the cross-examination of Mr. Moerbauer by my learned friend Mr. Moran. Here is why I raise this point with you. At that page, 3779, line 10, Mr. Moran asks Moerbauer: "It is not hard for a trained police officer to count from 1 to 51, is it?" At that point, Mr. Niemann objected. At the bottom of that page, beginning at line 22, Mr. Niemann said: "It is absurd to be putting these questions to this witness. Counsel knows the answer clearly. Everybody else in this courtroom knows the answer." With all due respect to my friend Mr. Moran, I agree with the Prosecutor. Police officers do know how to count. My final remarks on these videos is the point raised on having shown a video to a witness that has taken place in this courtroom. Of course, that proves absolutely nothing with regard to the provenance of a videotape. More specifically, the portion of video shown to Dr. Grubac and Dr. P, interview conducted, is Zvonko Maric and Jadranka Milosevic; your Honours, the original footage shown to these two witnesses was provided to the Delalic Defence by the journalists themselves, by Maric and Milosevic. Indeed it was the Delalic Defence who provided that videotape through discovery to the Prosecution. That does not -- that is not footage from the tape I46. That was provided by the Defence to the Prosecution. So to sum up, your Honours, there is no confusion on the part of the police. The record is clear. They can count, they did count, they counted differently. These videotapes therefore have not been authenticated, the relevancy is not shown and they are of little or no probative value and for those reasons we respectfully submit that they should be excluded from evidence. The second point I would like to briefly address your Honours on is in relation to Exhibit 130, which my friend Mr. Greaves made the central document to his submissions. I will not repeat the Articles and the Rules to which he referred, those being 21, 20, Rule 89 and Rule 95, but I would add just one point with regard to the position of Mr. Delalic in this document. This document, of course, purports to be a letter of Mr. Mucic, which allegedly presents an account of matters in 1992. We say that if your Honours should rule this document admissible, and should you decide that it is Mr. Mucic's document under Article 21(4)G, Mr. Mucic, of course, cannot be compelled to give testimony and the consequence of that for Mr. Delalic is that under Article 21(4)E Mr. Delalic is deprived of his right to cross-examine. Similar argumentation given by Mr. Greaves on the general nature of this, I wish to reiterate it on behalf of Mr. Delalic, that the admissibility of this document would gravely impact upon his rights under Article 20 and Article 21, and therefore we respectfully submit that this Exhibit 130 should be excluded on the basis of Rule 89 and Rule 95. At this point, my learned colleague Madam Residovic will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respects, your Honours, I wish to remind you that making my objections up to document 125 as submitted by the Prosecutor, I presented the arguments why these documents should not be admitted into evidence. Appreciating the time devoted to this important issue, and in order to avoid repeating with respect to each document which is beyond doubt and clear, I wish in connection with all the other documents, before passing on to more specific objections, I wish to say the following: first, the Prosecution has not managed to prove that any one of the documents offered to the court comes from the search in INDA-BAU. Witness Moerbauer, as you will recall, and the Prosecution referred to his testimony, indicating the pages and lines of their testimony in the transcript, said only that he had received from witness Navrat some binders, and this witness later, several days after having received this cardboard box from witness Navrat, analysed those documents, and all that we have in the testimony of this witness is the Bericht, or rather his analysis, dated 22nd and 26th April, when he submitted that analysis to the Austrian court. Therefore the period from 18th March until the end is a period within which we are unable closely to follow the fate of the folders, and still less of the contents of those folders. In accordance with your instructions, your Honours, which I referred to earlier on, the Prosecution also called the witness who seized the evidence from INDA-BAU. Witness Navrat stated clearly that he did not on the spot mark a single document. This witness did not recognise any single document, and furthermore witness Moerbauer, who did the analysis, testified before the court that all the markings that he personally put on the documents during his analysis had disappeared, and that he personally was unable to recognise here in court any one of those documents, because he does not know Bosnian, because he could not find his markings, and he never had any expert analysis of any handwriting. Therefore the first question that applies to all the documents proposed by the Prosecution is that the Prosecution has not in any way provided proof of the source of these documents, that is the place from which these documents come. Regarding the authenticity of documents, it is also necessary for the Prosecution to show us who is the author of which document. Unfortunately, in a very lengthy analysis of individual documents and comparing them with others, the Prosecution has failed to provide a single element of proof which could confirm in a method that would be appropriate who is the author of any one single document being offered. I shall now try to group some of those documents, but before that, let me say with respect to documents that I cannot put in a group, let me comment on them first. A document that I have not commented on was document 127. Could I please be allowed to analyse that document? You know that it is an order dated 3rd June 1992, containing certain facts in connection with the establishment of a railway line, and traffic along it. Comparing this document with other documents, the Prosecutor is trying to lead you to believe that the co-ordinator has certain command authority. I should like to remind you of the testimony of General Divjak, who was shown this document, and who made a distinction before you here, between Neretva and Naredjenje and order and command, and then also stated clearly that the signature and function of co-ordinator does not have any value as an order or any authority to issue orders, that the co-ordinator is only a person who mediates and can sign a document in that capacity. I also wish to draw your attention to a document admitted by this Trial Chamber, and issued by the supreme staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina and signed by army general Rasim Delic, according to which a co-ordinator in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not have any command, but only an mediatory role. The command function rests with the bodies which appointed that co-ordinator. In view of the fact that there is no thread, that the Prosecutor is referring to, this document has no relevance with regard to the position of my client and particularly not any relevance to the indictment that is before the Trial Chamber. Therefore, regardless of where that document comes from, and I have already said that we do not know the source, nor do we have any evidence to prove that it comes from INDA-BAU, this document has no probative value, nor relevance with respect to the indictment, its relevance is zero. The next document which the Prosecution try to prove the authenticity and reliability of is document 128. If you recall, your Honours, it is the request for conducting investigations against Mr. Zejnil Delalic and Mr. Zdravko Mucic, and as you will also recall, this document, as well as the criminal charges recognised by General Pasalic, was tendered for its limited scope, that is from the position of the functions held by those persons. Allow me, your Honours, unlike the Prosecutor who tried to prove the limited probative value of this document, he linked it with other documents pursuing the thread as my learned friend likes to say; let me add the following: precisely in connection with that limited scope, not only of this document but also of the documents number 137, 141 and 125, and these are -- I apologise, my client has just had a suggestion to convey to me and I apologise for the interruption. This document linked to these other documents, that is numbers 125, 141 and 137, show exactly to what extent these documents would be unreliable even within their limited scope; namely, can these documents show at all what position and function was held by my client in the relevant period. If you remember the document report to the general staff which was shown to General Pasalic, in which certain positions were indicated, you will see immediately that in that document the person who will later be used as one who could authenticate a document, that is Edib Saric, that person is mentioned in the document as assistant commander, and in the document that has been admitted into evidence we will see -- that is the document dated 14th August -- Edib Saric appears as a person appointed as deputy commander of Tactical Group 2, the commander of which is Husein Alic. Then we see again that this name appears on 20th August as assistant for security affairs in the temporary command group JUG, and then in the exhibit of the Prosecutor dated 24th November 1992, this same person appears as assistant commander in the operative group. When all these documents were shown to the witness General Pasalic, he stated that when he was compiling the report for the supreme command on 7th December he had no documents or evidence as to the functions and positions held by individual people listed in this document. Therefore, this document in itself cannot be indicative of the positions and functions of any one of those persons mentioned in the document or any others. Document 128 is quite in contrast with the claims in the criminal charges identified by General Pasalic as criminal charges submitted by the 4th Corps. No one -- comparing these two documents alone, you will see, your Honours, that the position of Mr. Delalic on 31st May is quite contrary to the position indicated in this document, and later on in the document dropping charges, that same function will not appear. Therefore the reasons why this is being offered as relevant evidence are also highly problematic, and the relevance of these documents outside that limited scope does not exist with respect to the charges contained in the indictment. Your Honours, shall I continue or would it be convenient to have a break now before going on to the next document I wish to comment on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will have a break and come back at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, how much longer are we to expect you to address us, because we are not sitting tomorrow, and we are likely to be off for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you put it yourself, and the Prosecutor also mentioned it, these are important documents. As I said, I am going to attempt to group the documents and present them in that manner. I know that you are not asking this question to limit me in any way, but at this point, I cannot tell you precisely how much time, but what I am going to try to do is to group the document and to be very concise in presenting my arguments and only where I must -- where I feel I need to be present an individual document, I will do that. I am sorry that I cannot give you a precise answer. This will take a while. I would like to finish it today. However, if I do not manage to do that, the arguments will have to continue thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I was just trying to alert you as to what perhaps you might face in terms of time. It is not to compel you to change your style, but just to make you know what you might face. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may Ms. McMurrey have leave to depart at 5.10? She has some obligations outside the Tribunal she needs to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She is free to be discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May I continue now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My presentation hereafter is facilitated by the fact that the majority of the legal arguments which I had in mind have already been presented by my colleagues, and as I pointed out before, I will just try to point out some of these arguments in connection with the groups of documents that I am trying to present. The Prosecutor presented as evidence a number of documents that have a look of official documents. I have only analysed some of them. As my learned colleague Greaves said, I would like to restate some of these things in regard to these documents. We do not know where they come from. We do not know their authenticity, whether it is real or not. There is only one way to determine this, to call the representatives of the institutions as we have already tried the best we could in cases of some documents by certain Bosnian authorities; in other words, we would like to call the representatives of these institutions before this Tribunal, so that they may be able to authenticate these documents. As I said, I do not need to repeat the stamp and everything else that surrounds this document. This is not possible to fabricate, forge. Some of these documents are in handwriting. There are quite a few of such documents, I have not counted them, but among the ones that we have not presented arguments on, there are nine, and I do not wish to analyse these nine documents for you, your Honours, and show for each one that the thread referred to by the Prosecutor, with respect to their authenticity, exists or not. The position of the Delalic Defence is that this thread does not exist. With respect to the remaining hand-written documents, I will remind you of the arguments by my learned colleagues which point out that some of these hand-written documents, for some of these documents the Prosecutor claims that they were written by some third persons and for some documents, he is trying to say that they were written by my client. He has not shown who actually wrote these documents or those submissions or those papers, or parts thereof. He has not demonstrated in any real way where these documents come from, where they were compiled. He did not show what the value of these documents is or who they belong to. From all these documents, I am only going to point out two. One of them is the document 126, which was written 27th April 1993, according to the document. This is the document which was created much later than the events that are covered in the indictment. The value that the Prosecutor sees in this document is that it speaks to the conflict of the HVO and the BH, the possible development, possible agreement of Milosevic and Tudjman, of the possibility of certain events happening, so there are no references to my client whatsoever; there are no references in it to the charges against my client or any other client in the indictment, and there is even a further problem with this document. If you look at the first paragraph, it speaks of some persons who allegedly went to Czechoslovakia, so we could rightly ask; does this document come from Czechoslovakia? Was it created there and somehow found its way to the Prosecution and was presented here? The next hand-written document is the document 131. You will recall this document, it is entitled "The Adventurer". Could the technical booth please display this document 131 in its Bosnian version, so that we could see how these documents look, these documents presented by the Prosecution, with the intent to show its authenticity and reliability. My colleague Ackerman made an example of how such a document could be found in a garbage bin, where somebody could have put down in writing his musings, and the Prosecution shows us this document, not only analysing it but contending that this document was written, which was written in the third person singular, written by the deputy commander of Tactical Group 1, and I would like the next page of this document to be shown, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you think we need to go through this exercise? Do you think it is necessary? You may if you wish, but I do not think it explains more than has been explained before now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am talking about the threads pointed to by the Prosecutor and I think that the Prosecutor had enough time to present these threads in the last three days. I am hoping that I will be able to present my arguments very concisely. I would only like to show these two hand-written documents, and I think that I can draw several conclusions and arguments. I will bear in mind your remark not to repeat things, but I would just like to make things more concise and clear. I think that this was the nature of your remark to me now, and I am grateful for it. May I continue, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document as we are showing now -- and the argument if a knife or a bullet could be found, and I do not think that this is either a knife or a bullet situation, I think that analysis and expertise would have to be made to authenticate who compiled this document. In connection with the documents that are in the handwriting, I know that my colleague Mr. Niemann knows the geography of the Balkans much better than I know the geography of Australia, but his remark when he tried to compare in this document the mention of Donje Selo, this is compared to the document in Dugo Selo, there was a barracks there. This barracks was in Dugo Selo, it is in Croatia, it is a different country, and Donje Selo is a geographic settlement that was in the Neretva river valley, part of the Konjic municipality. So we cannot accept those kinds of arguments as authentic and as credible. I am trying, your Honour, to only point to certain documents and to point out a larger general problem in the entire argumentation, but not to interconnect these documents with other documents and other facts. These are all facts in the transcript and in evidence. The next group of the documents relates to the contention of the Prosecutor that the authenticity and reliability of these documents -- that my client Mr. Zejnil Delalic did recognise some of the documents presented. This is the order of 11th July, because there was a certain lengthy debate that surrounded this document, and it was not shown to my -- the document that my client was shown was not from INDA-BAU but from Munich. It was 1290. This was a fax that came from Munich and it points to the difficulties of communication between Sarajevo and the region where my client was. Another document from the group that was shown to my client have not been offered here to this Trial Chamber, and from the transcript of these questioning in Scheveningen, it shows that I have submitted personally this document on behalf of my client, so I am pointing to this document as -- all this points to the fact that all documents offered in this group have such limited value of authenticity that they cannot be offered in evidence. During the seizure of documents, over 12,770 documents were seized. Mistakes were made during the seizure and transfer of documents. Some documents were photocopied and taken away without a court's approval, and there are testimonies by Moerbauer, d’Hooge and other Austrian policemen which were brought to testify here, and the Prosecutor himself does not know the provenance of some of the documents that found their way into the files. I am pointing, your Honours, to the statement of the witness Panzer when he was cross-examined by my colleague with respect to the green file folder. The witness Panzer said: "My colleague Moerbauer and I made this green file folder. We put there different papers and there were a number of them." I remind you, your Honours, that in the Niederschrift from INDA-BAU, where allegedly all these documents were marked, it states that 12 file folders were taken there. There are no loose papers there and the testimony of Panzer before this Tribunal clearly points that there is no reliable way to test reliability of this evidence, of these documents which would have to have a certain amount of relevance. In conclusion, your Honours, I would like to point out some documents which have been tendered here and offered in evidence. The Prosecutor offers as a document that was already recognised by my client a booklet on the Green Berets, and also a letter which he does not know whether it was found in the Prosecution files in the original or not. He says that the organisation was founded in 1994, and the document clearly gives the date of 15th January 1992. So it is clear that this document has no value, without being submitted to the kind of test that my colleagues have talked about. There is another document that my client has allegedly recognised. This is regarding his membership in the SDA, and in the interview in Scheveningen, my client is explaining the situation that the club in Vienna is no political party. Witness Panzer confirmed this, because he said that no foreign political parties can be active in Austria. A copy of this document, dated 18th March, shows again how unreliable this alleged "thread" that the Prosecutor talks about is, because according to the testimony of witness Panzer, who said that he immediately placed these documents under lock, Mr. Moerbauer who copied a few things and Mr. d’Hooge, they all said that nobody put any markings on it, and there is a date of 18th March on it. Is it possible that another document from Munich, where my client was arrested that day, and where it was possible that this membership card would be, could it be that this document could be placed -- of that date could be placed on a document then? So it is again very obvious that the reliability of this document is very questionable. Then we have a copy of a questionnaire, who when asked by my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan was not able to be authenticated. It was not clear whether it was a copy which was attached to another document, and apparently there are a number of facts displayed there that are supposedly true. The Prosecutor had to have -- the Prosecutor did not prove any facts from this document, whether that my client was decorated with the fleur-de-lis, whether he spoke Romanian, et cetera et cetera. So this document could have been compiled at any time. Your Honours, I wholly agree with the arguments presented by my colleagues, and I am sure that in the interests of right and justice you will come to the conclusion that the Prosecution was unable to prove the reliability and authenticity of these documents, that the Prosecution, for all these documents, has not proven their relevance and their probative value. All this, based on Rule 89 and Rule 95, I move that these documents as proposed by the Prosecutor not be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Moran, have you anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If it please the court, I would like to divide the argument into basically four areas. The first thing is I would like to wax a little bit eloquent, like my friends Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Greaves did, about the evidence; then I would like to go to a little bit about the threads that the Prosecutor has talked about, and I will show you why the threads are not there; then there are three or four individual documents, I will discuss why they should not be admitted, at least against my client Mr. Delic, and finally I would like to have about two minutes of the court's time on a personal matter. With that I begin. The Prosecutor has talked about the court being made up of professional judges and that you can sort it through and throw out what you want, and has cited a couple of times the Krupp case, which is one of the post-World War II tribunals under control counsel law 10. Given Judge McDonald's plurality decision in Erdemovic, I do not know how much precedential value any of those control counsel 10 cases have, but that is neither here nor there. My discussion is this: all of the post-World War II tribunals, Nuremberg, Tokyo, the control counsel 10 cases and the Yomashada case operated under a set of rules of evidence that were imposed upon the judges by an outside source, and they were all fairly identical. Basically, you could look at the rules -- and they are set out, the Yomashada rules are set out in a footnote in that case, the rules of evidence, and basically it said anything the Prosecutor wants to come in can come in. He could use sworn depositions, even though there was no right of cross-examination. The judges were required to admit as substantive evidence any report by a government agency of any government of the then United Nations, which refers to the allies in World War II. In fact, in the Nuremberg case, that evidence was used to admit a report from the Soviet government into the murder of 10,000 Polish officers which the Germans were charged with doing, and in fact a few months ago President Yeltsin said the Russians had done. Those rules of evidence, which by the way were imposed on the American zonal courts, control counsel 10 courts, under Ordinance 7, were strongly criticised, I believe it was the hostages case, it may very well have been the List case, where the court essentially said, "you can admit this stuff, but you cannot make us give it any weight. It is our business how much weight we give it". I would suggest, especially in the light of Yomashada, which was not one of the greater days for the Supreme Court of the United States, that when the Security Council set up this Tribunal, it adopted Article 15 of the Statute, which instead of imposing rules of evidence on the court from an outside source said that the judges should be imposing these rules of evidence. The court has adopted, what is it, 11 Rules of Evidence in total, that also say that you can look to the national rules of evidence, which brings me directly to document number 130, which purports to be -- Prosecution Exhibit 130 purports to be a statement from Pavo Mucic in which he inculpates my client. I do not know whether that is a statement by Mr. Mucic or whether it is not a statement by Mr. Mucic. As to the general admissibility of it, I will leave that to Mr. Greaves and Mr. Olujic. What I would suggest is this: some weeks and months ago, I filed a memorandum of law with the court citing a case called R v Silcott, a British case, and several cases from the Supreme Court of the United States on the admissibility of co-defendants' statements against those defendants. It was done at the time that the custodial statements were admitted some months ago, and I think the holding of the court was at that point that a defendant's statement is admissible against that defendant and nobody else, and I would ask the court to continue that ruling as it applies to Prosecution Exhibit 130. Moving along to Prosecution exhibit -- my notes have it in Prosecution Exhibit 126. This relates directly to a question Judge Jan asked I believe yesterday, or the day before, about the date of creation of Tactical Group 1. The Prosecution exhibit, I believe it is 118, which is the orders assigning Mr. Delalic to command that, show that he was replacing someone else, so we do not know when TG1 was created, but we know that it was probably before 11th July. However, Prosecution Exhibit 128 refers to an incident which occurred prior -- that is a report involving the murder of a man named Bubalo. All the acts occurred prior to July 11th, as laid out in that report, and gives various positions that people held at the time of the incident. Clearly when it says that Mr. Delalic was not -- was the commander of TG1 in June, we know that that is wrong, so these kinds of threads start falling apart when people start pulling on them, judge, these threads of admissibility the Prosecutor talks about. Prosecution Exhibit 129 seems to be some kind of an investigation report. This, I would submit, would be very similar to the report of that Soviet commission into the deaths of the Polish officers at the Nuremberg case. It is totally lacking in reliability. We do not know who did this report, who they did it for; there are three people that signed it, surely one of them can be found in order to come down and testify to those facts. There is no way to cross-examine them. Prosecution Exhibit 131. That is the "Adventurer" letter. There are two problems I see with that letter, and I will suggest this to the court. I am not suggesting anything sinister on the part of anyone; however, every document that we have seen has what we call in America a BATES stamp. It is a serial number, an 8-digit number that appears on every document that the Prosecutor has handed us. The Bosnian original has a set of BATES numbers on Prosecution Exhibit 131, and when you go to the English translation, it lists down at the bottom -- in fact if the technical people could put it up, the English translation, at the very bottom it says, "end of page number" and lists a 7-digit number on the first page, and then on the second page of the English translation of Exhibit 131, it lists another 7-digit number at the end of that page. Those numbers are different from the BATES stamp numbers on the original Bosnian document. I cannot explain it. I do not speak Bosnian, and I am just suggesting that the court ought to take a look at that, of the reliability at least of the translation. Prosecution Exhibit 135, I suggest again the Prosecutor keeps talking about these threads of evidence. Prosecution 135 purports to be a SDA Party card issued in Vienna on May 4th 1992 to Mr. Delalic. Wherever Zejnil Delalic was on May 4th 1992, he was not in Vienna, he was in Bosnia, that is what all the evidence is. Prosecution Exhibit 143. We do not know what that is. It purports to be a press release of some kind, a press statement. We do not know who did it, we do not know where it came from, it is not on any kind of letterhead. Prosecution Exhibit 146, the "Hazim" memo. Again, I do not want to speak to the general admissibility of that, but I would object to it being admitted against my client on the theory that (i) we do not know who Hazim is, and although the Prosecutor asserts it is Hazim Delic, but (ii) there is no way of showing he knew of its existence until he arrived at The Hague as a prisoner. We do know for a good portion of the time after December 1992 Mr. Delic was either being incarcerated in a manhole at Celebici or in some other prison, including the Celebici prison and the Musala sports hall and would probably have no way of contacting anyone to learn about this. With that, I would adopt the statements of my -- the objections of my friends, and if the court would indulge me for about a minute or two, there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Going outside the discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. On more of a personal matter. There is a very, very real possibility that I will not be here on November 24th, and I just did not want to leave, with a 50/50 chance I will not be back I would feel horrible if I did not say goodbye to the court. It is a personal and professional thing, having absolutely nothing to do with anyone who is a member in this room, but over the months we have been here, I have learned to admire the court and learned to like them, as we got to know each other better. I would say if I do not return, I would have felt very bad if I did not say goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean you are doubting whether you will come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a 50/50 chance that I will not be returning, based on various personal and professional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: At this stage I think that is a little unfortunate, if you have got to this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will take note of it, but I do not know. We will take note of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, in the chance that I do not return, I want to wish you all very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We do hope that you return, I think. We will need you to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that makes me feel very good to hear you say that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, have you any few areas to touch on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, if I may first address the question of the general submissions that were made to you by Mr. Greaves and Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Ackerman urged your Honours to look at this whole question of documentary evidence and to provide this jurisdiction with an opinion which could have application and benefit for future cases that would come before the Chamber. We would urge your Honours to do that too, but we would urge your Honours to do it on the basis of the rules that your Honours have developed in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and having regard to the Statute. This jurisdiction, your Honours, is not the same as a national jurisdiction. It is not correct to say that you should have regard to the rules of evidence of a national jurisdiction when dealing with questions of admissibility. Your Honours are aware that in national jurisdictions, in some national jurisdictions, they vary, difficulties have arisen in relation to documents, and primarily because you are dealing with documents as hearsay. There is no question, your Honours, that a document is hearsay. It is hearsay evidence. It is not correct to say that documents should not be admitted into evidence because it offends the right that may be given to an accused to cross-examine witnesses under Article 21 of the Statute. Of course the accused has a right to confront the witnesses that testify against him, and has the right to cross-examine, but it is a misconstruction, in my submission, to then say that that guarantee applies across the board to all facets of evidence, including documents themselves. Documents are, and have been always recognised as hearsay. They are an exception to the hearsay rule, and in fact, your Honours, in some common law jurisdictions the evolution of the process of dealing with documentary evidence has come about with an enormous amount of legislation which has attempted to ameliorate the old common law provisions that applied to them. Your Honours, the old common law principle of calling the author of the document, and that being the only basis upon which a document is admitted into evidence practically has no application in any jurisdiction in the world any more. There are enormous legislative steps that have been taken since those days when that was the rule of the common law. There are considerable exceptions that go to tendering documents, such as business records provisions, such as computer records, such as the records of government departments, such as official publications, such as certificates issued, and all of these have been dealt with by way of legislation. Your Honours devised a set of rules to deal with the admissibility of evidence, and Rule 89 is in very simple terms. You were taken to it by Mr. Greaves, and he said to you that when looking at that Rule your Honours should -- either Mr. Greaves or Mr. Ackerman -- your Honours should devise a set of rules which properly reflect the necessity for you to determine a fair trial, and we would not quarrel with that for one minute. But in this jurisdiction there is also a balance, and a balance has been introduced because of the necessity to have regard to the interests of victims and witnesses and to have regard to the overall operation of this Tribunal in the jurisdiction in which it functions. Your Honours, the primary consideration is pursuit of the truth. If your Honours have any doubt about documents, if your Honours are uncomfortable about any documents, you should not rely upon them. You should not accept them, you should reject them. You should do so if you feel that that would in any way encroach upon the necessity for you to ensure that a fair trial is had by the accused. But by the same time, the Statute and the Rules require you to have consideration to the broader interests as well, the interests of victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, this raises another principle. Can a document be used against an accused when the purported author of that document is sitting in the court, but the accused cannot cross-examine him, cannot question him about the recitals he has made in that statement? The rule of fairness would not come in in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your Honour talking about the witness Ramic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am talking about the letter purporting to have been written by Mucic. Delalic is not in the position to cross-examine him, to question him about the contents of that document. Is it fair to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It falls into the same category as all documents, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Against whom the recitals in the document are to be used cannot question him. I am talking about the principle of fairness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, your Honours. In circumstances where you may, for example, have a conspiracy count to be considered, and where the parties get together, a group of co-offenders get together and conspire, and evidence of that conspiracy is presented in the form of documentary evidence, a similar situation may well apply there, that the document -- is it a document to be admitted against one party or admitted against a group? Your Honours may have to make that determination. You may have to do it on the basis of fairness; is it fair that it should apply that way? Your Honours, in our submission, there is no rule that says that your Honours cannot apply it. The principle that guides you all along is the interests of a fair trial, and it can be to do it. It is not necessarily unfair. As a question of principle, your Honours, what we urge you to do is to have regard to it, consider it and make the determination on that basis of a fair trial, and if your Honours believe that the evidence can be admissible against a co-accused in these circumstances and still represent a fair trial, then it should be applied for that purpose, but your Honours, it is not correct to say that simply because cross-examination cannot happen in relation to a document that that is the end of the matter and that a fair trial cannot be had. That is not the case in our submission at all. Your Honours could have numerous documents against people who are dead, people who cannot be brought before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The accused is prevented by law from asking questions from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be frustrating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am talking about fairness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be frustrating because the persons sits there and cannot be examined, but it is no different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am talking about fairness, not any other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is no different to a document that is admitted against somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because you see we have to ensure a fair trial, and I was just looking at it from that, because maybe it raises the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the other issue that has been raised in the course of the submissions is the reference to the fact that the documents need to be authenticated or proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and numerous times I have questioned this. A document, and we maintain that some of these documents fall into that category, are circumstantial evidence. It is the mass of which must be put together to produce the end result. Your Honours, circumstantial evidence is not, as some people might suggest it is, a link in a chain, so that if one of those links were to be taken, the chain would fall, not at all. Circumstantial evidence is like a thread in a rope. It can be insignificant in terms of its strength, but when put together with all the other threads, it receives its strength and may be used. I am not being original when I give this illustration, because it is an illustration that was given by an eminent jurist from the United Kingdom, Baron Pollock, but your Honours, it is a very appropriate, in my submission, analogy. When your Honours look at each one of these documents and each one of the submissions made, your Honours do not do it on the basis, "is this document the document that is going to determine the case on its own, it stands alone", the Prosecution tenders one document in a case, sits down and that is the end of the matter, because it does that exercise. That is not what we are doing or submitting. We are saying each must be considered. There is a process involved; the process is one of sifting and weighing, and your Honours may well, at the end of the day, reject some of the documents if you feel that either they are not of sufficient weight, or they do not have that reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I think the difficulty perhaps arises where it is the contents of the document themselves that is in issue, not the surrounding circumstances that a document has been produced. Those can give credible evidence of circumstantial evidence, that it could be done by such a person, but the truth of whether it was done is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours may well want reassurance when there are things in the documents that point to those conclusions. You may well want reassurance from other pieces of evidence. It may well be the case -- if your Honours were to rely on a document, one particular document as conclusive to a particular element of the offence, we do not quarrel with the fact that that document -- you would have to be satisfied that that document proves the issue beyond a reasonable doubt. We do not for one minute quarrel with that issue. So, your Honours, to address the general submission that is put to you, and having regard to the fact that the Rules of Evidence are what they are, it is our submission that your Honours have that very difficult task, to perform the function of judge and jury. In most jury jurisdictions, you have a situation where the trial judge receives the evidence, receives all of the evidence in the voir dire, determines the issue of admissibility and then proceeds for the matter to go to the jury. Your Honours must proceed to do both of those functions, and I am first to say that I think it is a difficult and complex function, and I sincerely hope that from both sides of the courtroom we have endeavoured to assist your Honours in the performance of that function, and it ultimately falls to your Honours to do so. Your Honours, with respect to the Nuremberg principles, I do not think it is fair to describe it as "any document that the Prosecution wants to be admitted gets admitted". It was not as broad as that at all. In fact, from my memory of the Nuremberg principles which I took your Honours to when I made that long submission about the admissibility of evidence, there was a remarkable similarity between the Rules of Evidence that your Honours have devised, in particular under Rule 89, and what then applied at Nuremberg. Principle objective, your Honours, is to seek out and obtain the truth. There are enough limitations upon your Honours in doing that in terms of the acquisition of physical evidence and the circumstances in any event. The creation of national rules of evidence relating to hearsay and so forth which would preclude your Honours from having access to this evidence cannot assist you in the task at the end of the day and in my submission, your Honours, has led you, as the judges in plenary, to devise Rules of Evidence which would best enable you to arrive at the truth of the matter. In our submission, they are Rule 89 and the other limited Rules of Evidence that are provided for in the rules. Your Honours, if you are to deal with this difficult issue, it is how those rules are best applied when weighing the necessity to ensure a fair trial, but so as to ensure that material comes before you for consideration, which is the hard task that you have to perform. It is not achieved, in our submission, your Honours, by simply picking up and applying the rules of evidence that relate to national jurisdictions, and which vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction where you have no benefit of a legislature to guide you in what rules of evidence should be applied. Your Honours have the difficult task, and it is a difficult task, of having a great deal more evidence to come before you than might come before a jury in a jury trial. It is a difficult task, but in our submission the rules are specifically designed to enable you to get at the truth and by getting at the truth, in our submission, you should not be hampered or prevented from seeing the evidence as it is. I do not wish to address your Honours specifically on each document, I have done that, but I am anxious to encourage your Honours to look at the rules, having regard to the way they are drafted and the way they should, in our submission, be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, an issue came up just now as a result of Judge Jan's question regarding co-defendants' statements, and then Mr. Niemann threw in the issue of conspiracy. May I have two minutes to address that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may, but I do not think it is really necessary. But you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can do it, I think, very quickly. The jurisdiction that I am from, federal prosecutors primarily are in love with conspiracy, so I have tried a number of conspiracy cases. Just as a general proposition, statements of co-defendants are not admissible against other defendants. That is frequently dealt with by severance, or the statement is not admitted in a situation where a jury or a judge could even begin to use it against another defendant. The exception to that is in a conspiracy case, where the defendants were seen during a certain period of time to have been acting together toward a common purpose, and the theory is that statements made by them during the course of that conspiracy and in furtherance of it are common statements that are attributable to all of them, and so those kind of statements would be admissible against each other. That situation ends when the conspiracy ends, and what frequently happens, when accusations are made against individuals who were alleged to have been acting together toward that common purpose. Once the conspiracy is over, frequently the motive is to exculpate themselves and inculpate the others, so any statement made following, like the Mucic statement in this case, much later, long after Celebici was closed, cannot have any reliability, because it can be seen as a statement designed to exculpate some and inculpate others and not something that was furthering any conspiracy that was going on, so that is the way -- I can only tell you how American courts view that. I have tried, I do not know, 100 conspiracy cases. The Mucic statement certainly would not be admissible against any other defendant in the United States, and in its current condition not even admissible against Mucic, because of the lack of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will have to conclude with one other matter which has been pending. I think that is the admissibility of Exhibit 155. We deferred the ruling on the request for the admissibility. The letter allegedly written by Mucic and for an order compelling him to produce a sample of his handwriting. We just want to give an oral ruling, the full decision will be published soon. The Trial Chamber has considered the two requests made by the Prosecution in connection with Exhibit 155. It is clear that the request called into consideration crucial issues in regard to the construction of various provisions of the Statute, and Rules of the International Tribunal, particularly those relating to the nature and ambit of the right of an accused person before the Tribunal, the standards for admissibility of evidence, and the powers of a Trial Chamber seized of a trial. The Trial Chamber has decided to grant the Prosecution's first request, namely that Exhibit 155 should be admitted in evidence. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the provisions under admissibility of evidence contained in Section 3 of the Rules are quite clear and unambiguous. The test for admissibility, in accordance with sub-rule 89C is that evidence is relevant and should have probative value. The Trial Chamber accepts that reliability is an inherent and implicit component of each of these elements of admissibility. It is indeed the invisible golden thread that runs through both components. However, it is neither necessary nor desirable to regard it as a separate milestone on the route to admissibility of evidence before the Trial Chamber. The arguments of both parties, admittedly to different ends, on the importance and need for reliability before evidence may be admitted are convincing and the Trial Chamber's written opinion expatiates on its reasons for coming to this conclusion. The letter on its own has sufficient relevance and probative value for admissibility. However, the claim by the Prosecution that the contents of the letter tend to prove certain elements of the indictment, because of its allegations, then the letter was written by Mucic, have not been sufficiently proven. The Prosecution has not established a sufficient nexus between its contents and Mucic. It is therefore admitted only to the extent to which evidence of its existence has been laid before the Trial Chamber. That is as a letter being of relevance to these proceedings, exhibiting probative value, and written to Witness B by an unknown third person. The question of the content of this letter, governed by proof of signature, is a matter that attaches to the weight to be given to the letter during the deliberations of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber is unable to grant the Prosecution's request for an order compelling the production of a handwriting sample from Mucic. The Trial Chamber is not satisfied that a handwriting sample per se can be regarded as forming material proof against an accused person. It is of the opinion that where the material elements add something to the elements incriminating an accused person, a sample of his handwriting -- to compel him to supply the sample which is the missing element would infringe the provisions of Article 21(4)G of the statute. The Trial Chamber rejects the Prosecution's contention that the handwriting will serve no purpose other than for identification. The reason for requiring the handwriting sample is clearly as admitted by the Prosecution; to ascertain conclusively the authorship of the letter. If authenticated, it will act as sufficient admission of its content in respect of counts on the indictment against the author. The obvious implication is that the accused will be compelled by an order of the Trial Chamber to assist the Prosecution in its investigation, and probably provide evidence to incriminate himself. The fact that a handwriting sample per se is trial evidence is not the issue. If the handwriting sample, taken together with other evidence, will constitute material evidence to prove the charge against the accused, then the order of the Trial Chamber would have compelled the production of self-incriminating evidence. There is no legal or moral duty on the accused to fill a vacuum created by an investigative gap of the Prosecution. Self-preservation is the first principle of life. It is an elementary principle of proof that he who alleges must prove the subject matter of his allegation. The Prosecution having alleged that Mucic authored Exhibit 155, has to discharge the burden of proof on it by the Defence. This is the ruling of the Trial Chamber. A reasoned written decision will follow shortly. Now we have a few difficulties, because we are not likely to sit until Monday, 1st December, because of difficulties in the position of the court itself, because other Trial Chambers will be taking over, sitting here. But when we do sit, we will sit until Friday, 5th December. During this week, we hope we will be able to have the two expert witnesses to testify, and hopefully Professor Economides is to be cross-examined and Dr. Gow is to testify in chief. We are hoping that perhaps we will conclude all those proceedings within the period. After that period, I think we are not likely to recommence until Monday, 12th January. The Trial Chamber will appeal to the Defence to start its preparations for presentation of its case, so that we will not have an undue delay after the conclusion of the case of the Prosecution. They should be able to get their case together in general so we can proceed. I think to a large extent we still need Mr. Niemann to show us when he is closing his case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is our expectation, your Honour, that we will finish on that week, the week of the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The first week in December. We expect you to be able to say something. It is just to give notice to the Defence so that they know they have to organise themselves, carry on immediately. We return in January. I think this is all we have for the day. (5.40 pm)
